description: Largest European polity of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries (c. 1236–1569) stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea; its pagan ruling dynasty's 1386 conversion to Latin Christianity secured the Jagiellonian dynastic union with Poland and a formidable alliance against the Teutonic Order, while its multicultural character, Lithuanian, Ruthenian, and Polish, made it a unique constitutional experiment.

temporal.notes: Largest medieval European state by territory at 1430s peak

lifecycle_phases.description: Mindaugas unifies the Lithuanian tribal confederation and is briefly baptized, receiving a royal crown from Pope Innocent IV (1253) before reverting to paganism. Lithuania remains the last major pagan state in Europe. It survives Teutonic Order crusades by incorporating Ruthenian principalities (former Kievan Rus lands devastated by the Mongols), giving Lithuania Slavic administrative personnel and Orthodox Christian subjects.

Gediminas (1316–1341) establishes Vilnius as the capital and dramatically expands eastward into the power vacuum left by the Mongol destruction of Kievan Rus. Algirdas (1345–1377) doubles the duchy's territory, reaching the Black Sea. By 1380 Lithuania controls more of former Kievan Rus territory than any other state, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea.

Jogaila accepts Catholic baptism and marries Hedwig of Poland (Union of Krewo, 1385), becoming King of Poland as Władysław II Jagiełło while remaining Grand Duke of Lithuania. The combined Polish-Lithuanian forces defeat the Teutonic Order decisively at Grunwald/Tannenberg (1410). The Jagiellonian dynasty rules Poland-Lithuania as a major European power; the personal union gradually deepens toward a real union (completed 1569).

rise_factors.description: The Mongol destruction of Kievan Rus principalities (1237–1241) created a political vacuum in eastern Europe that Lithuania filled; the weakened Russian principalities accepted Lithuanian overlordship as preferable to Mongol domination

Lithuanian military forces combined the heavy cavalry tradition of the Ruthenian principalities with Lithuanian light cavalry and infantry; the defeat of the Teutonic Order at Grunwald (1410) was one of the largest battles in medieval European history

The Gediminid dynasty's flexibility, tolerating Orthodox Christianity among Ruthenian subjects while accepting Latin Christianity for western relations, allowed Lithuania to rule over ethnically and religiously diverse populations without triggering religious wars

Lithuanian warriors exploited dense Baltic forest terrain in guerrilla tactics against Teutonic Knights and Mongol raiders. Forest strongholds (pilys) enabled resistance that cost the Teutonic Order enormous resources.

Lithuanian grand dukes ruled a multi-confessional empire encompassing Orthodox Ruthenians, Catholic Poles, pagan Lithuanians, and Tatars. Relative religious tolerance retained loyalty of diverse subject populations.

The Battle of Grunwald/Žalgiris (1410), the largest land battle in medieval European history, crushed the Teutonic Order, ending its military expansion and making Lithuania-Poland the dominant Baltic power.
The Union of Krewo (1385) united Lithuania with Poland through Jogaila's marriage to Queen Jadwiga, creating a dynastic bloc that resisted both the Teutonic Order and Muscovite expansion.

decline_factors.description: Lithuanian noble (boyar) power constrained ducal authority; repeated succession disputes between Gediminid princes created civil wars that the Teutonic Order and later Moscow exploited

Grand Principality of Moscow's claim to be the protector of all Orthodox Christians gave it ideological grounds to absorb Lithuanian-controlled Orthodox Ruthenian territories, leading to persistent border wars.

Lithuania was the last European state to officially Christianize (1387), giving the Teutonic Order decades of crusade ideology to justify attacks. The conversion removed this pretext but left Lithuania late in building church-state administrative structures.
